picks.why: The family distillery William Grant built in Dufftown, whose first spirit ran on Christmas Day 1887. The 12 Year Old, at 40% ABV, has headed the range since it replaced the old unaged bottling in 2000, and it is a single malt a guest new to Scotch will often name.
picks.note: The label currently styles the bottling as Our Original Twelve or 12 Year Old depending on market; confirm the wording on the current label. The 2000 change from a non age statement bottling rests on one reference source; confirm. Library holds Glenfiddich.

picks.why: George Smith took out a licence for his still in the glen of the Livet in 1824, after the Excise Act of 1823 made legal distilling worth doing, and the distillery has worked almost without a break since. The 12 Year Old, matured in European and then American oak and bottled at 40% ABV, is the soft, fruity Speyside benchmark.
picks.note: Keep the licence claim narrow: the producer says the first legal licence in the parish of Glenlivet; some sources say the first in Speyside or in Scotland, which is not agreed. In the United States the bottle is labelled 12 Year Old Double Oak; confirm which label the Ledger prints. Library holds no Glenlivet record.

picks.flagship: The Macallan Sherry Oak 12 Years Old
picks.why: The Craigellachie distillery dated to 1824 whose house style is built on oak casks seasoned with sherry in Jerez. Sherry Oak 12, at 40% ABV, is the bottling that teaches what sherry seasoned oak does to a Speyside malt: dried fruit, spice and a deep colour from the wood alone.
picks.note: The producer says predominantly sherry seasoned European oak; some retailers say exclusively, so do not write exclusively. Double Cask 12 (European and American sherry seasoned oak, 40%, launched 2016) is the more common bar bottle in some markets; the author may prefer it. Library holds The Macallan.

picks.why: The second distillery the Grants of Glenfiddich built in Dufftown, in 1892, beside the ruin of Balvenie Castle. DoubleWood, launched in 1993, spends its years in American oak and then about nine months in sherry casks, so it is the bottling that teaches what a cask finish is, at 40% ABV.
picks.note: Sources describe the finishing casks as Spanish oak or European oak ex Oloroso; keep it as sherry casks unless the producer's page settles it. The nine months is the usual figure and should be confirmed. The Balvenie's own floor maltings and coppersmiths are worth checking for the backstory.

picks.why: A Speyside distillery in the village of Aberlour, rebuilt by James Fleming in 1879, whose A'bunadh is matured only in Oloroso sherry casks and bottled at cask strength with no age statement, each batch numbered. It is the bottling that teaches cask strength in a sherried Speysider.
picks.note: Strength moves by batch, about 60% ABV; never print one figure. The founding year is disputed: 1879 under Fleming, or 1826 for an earlier distillery on the site; tell both or neither. Whether the casks are all first fill differs by source. A bar more often carries Aberlour 12 Year Old or 16 Year Old Double Cask Matured; the author may prefer one of those as the flagship, which this run did not search.

alternates.why: A Speyside distillery owned by one family, the Grants of Glenfarclas, since 1865; the 105, first released in 1968, is sherry cask malt bottled at 60% ABV, 105 British proof, with no age statement on the label.
A Speyside malt long tied to Johnnie Walker; not confirmed in this run, so confirm the bottling and its strength before use.

picks.why: A distillery at Tain on the Dornoch Firth, founded in 1843, whose stills have necks over five metres high, which gives a light, floral spirit. The Original, ten years in ex bourbon American oak at 40% ABV, is the clean Highland malt and the reference for what bourbon casks alone give.
picks.note: Recent labels may carry no age statement although the producer still says ten years; confirm the label as it now reads before printing 10 Years Old. Keep the stills as a measured fact (5.14 m necks per the owner group), not a ranking.

picks.why: A small distillery in the middle of the West Highland port of Oban, where the Stevenson brothers, who built the town, began distilling in 1794. The 14 Year Old, at 43% ABV, has been the Western Highland bottling of Diageo's Classic Malts since that series began, and it is the coastal Highland malt a guest asks for by name.
picks.note: The Classic Malts launch is given as 1987, 1988 or 1989 by different sources; leave the year out. The founders' names are given as John and Hugh Stevenson, sometimes with James; the dates of their ownership differ by source.

picks.why: A distillery at Alness on the Cromarty Firth, founded by Alexander Matheson in 1839 and later run by the Mackenzies, whose clan stag is on every bottle. The 12 Year Old splits its spirit between ex bourbon casks and Oloroso sherry butts before marrying them, at 40% ABV: the rich, sherried Highland malt.
picks.note: Sources say the stag has been on the bottle since 1867; confirm. The sherry butts are said to have held a named aged Oloroso; confirm on the producer's page before naming the bodega. Sherry Cask Select is a separate 12 at a higher strength; do not confuse them.

picks.why: A distillery at about 1,073 feet in the Central Highlands, built in 1897 with spirit first run in 1898, in the pass on the road from Perth to Inverness. The 15 Year Old, at 43% ABV, is its Classic Malts bottling: a gentle, honeyed Highland malt that a guest who wants no smoke will often name.
picks.note: Not in the style's benchmarks today; chosen over Glengoyne and Edradour because it is a Classic Malt a working bar is likelier to carry. The altitude claim varies (highest or second highest working distillery, depending on Braeval); keep to the height in feet and avoid a ranking.

picks.why: A distillery at Brora in Sutherland, built in 1967 beside the site first worked in 1819, whose spirit is known for a waxy texture and goes largely into Johnnie Walker blends. The 14 Year Old, released as an official bottling in 2002 at 46% ABV, is the malt that teaches texture as a distillery character.
picks.note: The share that goes to Johnnie Walker (about 95%) rests on one source; leave the figure out or confirm. The old distillery became Brora; the renaming year differs by source. Some old listings give 43%; current bottlings are 46%, confirm.

alternates.why: A Highland distillery north of Glasgow owned by Ian Macleod Distillers, known for drying its malt without peat; the 12 Year Old was not confirmed in this run, so confirm before use.
A Perthshire Highland distillery, the malt at the heart of Dewar's; not confirmed in this run, so confirm the bottling and its strength before use.

picks.why: The distillery at Carbost on Loch Harport, Isle of Skye, founded by Hugh and Kenneth MacAskill about 1830. The 10 Year Old, bottled at 45.8% ABV, is peppery, smoky and maritime, and it is the island malt that sits between Islay smoke and Highland sweetness.
picks.note: The founding year is given as 1830 or 1831, and whether Kenneth was a partner differs by source; keep it to about 1830 and Hugh MacAskill unless confirmed. The Islands are not a protected region: in law these distilleries are Highland; the group should say so.

picks.flagship: Highland Park 12 Year Old Viking Honour
picks.why: The distillery at Kirkwall on Orkney, dated to 1798 and to Magnus Eunson, which still turns part of its own malt on a floor and dries it over Orkney peat that smells of heather. The 12 Year Old Viking Honour, from sherry seasoned casks at 40% ABV, is the honeyed, gently smoky island malt.
picks.note: Magnus Eunson's link to the 1798 distillery is the producer's story; tell it as the producer's. The share of malt from its own floors is not confirmed. Library holds Highland Park.

picks.why: The one distillery on the Isle of Jura, at Craighouse: founded in 1810, closed in 1901 and rebuilt in 1963 by estate owners who wanted to keep people on the island. The 10 Year Old, bourbon cask malt finished in Oloroso butts at 40% ABV, is the light, lightly smoky island malt a guest often meets early.
picks.note: The label once read Isle of Jura; it now reads Jura, with the 10 Year Old styled Aged 10 Years on some labels; confirm the current wording. Owned by Whyte and Mackay; the parent above that is not needed in prose.

picks.why: Arran's single malt has been made at Lochranza in the north of the island since 1995; a second distillery at Lagg in the south now makes the peated spirit, which is why the first was renamed Lochranza. The 10 Year Old, bourbon and sherry cask malt at 46% ABV, non chill filtered and of natural colour, is the unpeated island malt.
picks.note: Sources give the first spirit as 29 June or 17 August 1995; keep it to 1995. The 10 Year Old's cask recipe is given differently by sources; confirm on the producer's page. Machrie Moor is Lochranza's peated label and Lagg its own; keep them out of this pick.

picks.why: The one distillery on the Isle of Mull, in the harbour town of Tobermory, dated to 1798. It sells its unpeated malt as Tobermory and its peated malt as Ledaig; the 12 Year Old, launched in 2019 after a two year closure at 46.3% ABV, is the unpeated house style.
picks.note: The 12 replaced the 10 Year Old; confirm it is still the core bottling. The 1798 date is the producer's; confirm. Ledaig 10 Year Old is offered as an alternate and should not stand in the same group as this pick, since both are one distillery.

alternates.why: Tobermory distillery's peated malt, sold under the distillery's old name; the 10 Year Old is bottled at 46.3% ABV and non chill filtered. Use only if Tobermory is not used, since they are one distillery.
Orkney's second distillery, unpeated, matured in American oak; the 10 Year Old appears in current retail and replaced the Skiren bottling, which this run could not confirm. Confirm before use.

picks.why: A distillery at Clydebank on the edge of Glasgow that distils all of its spirit three times, the old Lowland way, which gives a light, clean malt. The 12 Year Old, matured in bourbon and sherry casks at 40% ABV, is a Lowland malt a guest will often meet.
picks.note: The founding date (usually 1823) and Clydebank were not confirmed in this run; confirm. Retail copy says the only fully triple distilled single malt in Scotland; that is a ranking and may no longer hold (Rosebank and Hazelburn also triple distil); keep to what it does.

picks.why: A distillery by the Kinchie Burn at Pencaitland, about fifteen miles from Edinburgh, begun as Milton by the brothers John and George Rate in 1825 and licensed as Glenkinchie in 1837. The 12 Year Old, at 43% ABV, is the Lowland bottling of the Classic Malts: grassy, floral and soft.
picks.note: The link to Milton is called probable by one source; tell it with care. It replaced a 10 Year Old as the entry bottling; confirm the year if used.

picks.why: A distillery on the River Bladnoch near Wigtown in the far south west of Scotland, founded by John and Thomas McClelland in 1817, bought in 2015 and back in production in 2017 after a long closure. The 10 Year Old, bourbon cask malt at 46.7% ABV and non chill filtered, is its core bottling.
picks.note: Production restarted only in 2017, so a 10 Year Old sold in 2026 is drawn on stock distilled before the closure or bought in; the author must confirm what the bottle holds and say it plainly. Retail copy calls it the southernmost and the oldest Lowland distillery; keep out both rankings.

picks.why: A distillery in the East Neuk of Fife, opened in 2014 by the family behind the Wemyss Malts bottling house, which buys its barley from farms within about six miles. Doocot, at 46% ABV, non chill filtered, from mostly ex bourbon casks with some re charred wine barriques, is the flagship of a new Lowland that is not only Glasgow and Edinburgh.
picks.note: Not in the style's benchmarks. Doocot replaced Dream to Dram as the flagship in 2023; Dream to Dram is retired. The family members are living: keep their names out. The water source is given differently by sources; leave it out.

picks.why: A distillery built in 2017 beside the ruined abbey at Newburgh in Fife, where the Exchequer Roll of 1494 records malt sent to Friar John Cor to make aqua vitae, a record told as the start of Scotch whisky's written history. MCDXCIV, the year in Roman numerals, is its single malt at 46% ABV, first released in 2021.
picks.note: Not in the style's benchmarks. The label prints Lindores Lowland Single Malt Scotch Whisky MCDXCIV; confirm the exact form for the flagship field. One source wrongly says the abbey was founded in 1494; it was founded in 1191. Keep the 1494 record as a record, not as a first.

alternates.flagship: Rosebank aged releases from stock distilled before 1993
alternates.why: The Falkirk distillery closed in 1993 and revived by Ian Macleod Distillers, distilling again from 2023 with three stills and worm tubs; it has no age stated core bottling yet, so it is told as history and revival, and its current release must be confirmed.
The Lowland malt distillery William Grant built at Girvan; not confirmed in this run, so confirm the bottling and whether it is current before use.

picks.why: A distillery on the south coast of Islay set up by the brothers Alexander and Donald Johnston, officially from 1815, which still turns part of its own malt on a floor and dries it over Islay peat. The 10 Year Old is the medicinal, iodine smoky malt that teaches what peat means.
picks.note: The strength differs by market (40% in Britain, 43% in the United States, to be confirmed); none of this run's sources gave it. Most of the malt comes from Port Ellen maltings, not its own floors. The Royal Warrant is a fact about a living person's title; leave it out. Library holds Laphroaig.

picks.why: A distillery on Lagavulin Bay, officially founded by John Johnston in 1816 on a site said to have held illicit stills long before. The 16 Year Old, at 43% ABV, is the Islay bottling of the Classic Malts: deep, slow smoke rounded by age.
picks.note: Peter Mackie, who created the White Horse blend in 1890, owned it; a dead founder figure who may be named. Do not name the 1990s White Horse bottlings as current. Library holds Lagavulin.

picks.why: The third of the south coast Islay distilleries beside Laphroaig and Lagavulin, dated to 1815. The Ten, bottled at 46% ABV without chill filtration and introduced in 2000, is heavily peated yet citrus bright, the bottling that shows peat and sweetness together.
picks.note: The label prints Ardbeg Ten; some markets print 10 Years Old. Confirm. The 1997 purchase by Glenmorangie and the reopening were not confirmed in this run. Retail copy uses rankings (peatiest); keep them out. Library holds Ardbeg.

picks.why: The distillery in the island's main town, dated to 1779, which still floor malts about 40% of its own barley and ages whisky in its No. 1 Vaults, partly below sea level on Loch Indaal. The 12 Year Old, at 40% ABV, is the middle ground of Islay: smoke with honey and citrus.
picks.note: The producer calls Bowmore the first licensed distillery on Islay and No. 1 Vaults the oldest maturation warehouse; both are rankings the author should not repeat. The 40% floor maltings share and the 25 ppm peating rest on two sources; confirm.

picks.why: A distillery near Port Askaig on the Sound of Islay, founded by Hector Henderson in 1846, whose output goes mostly into Johnnie Walker blends. The 12 Year Old, at 43% ABV, is a lighter, oily, coastal peat smoke, the Islay malt a guest meets inside blends before they meet it alone.
picks.note: The 43% figure comes from a reference infobox; confirm on the label. The share kept as single malt (about 5%) rests on one source; leave it out or confirm.

alternates.why: The Rhinns of Islay distillery that makes its Bruichladdich range unpeated from Scottish barley; The Classic Laddie is bottled at 50% ABV. Its peated malts are Port Charlotte and Octomore.
An Islay distillery on the north east coast whose house malt is unpeated; the 12 Year Old has been bottled at 46.3% ABV without chill filtration or added colour since its 2010 relaunch.

picks.why: A Campbeltown distillery dated to 1828 and run by the Mitchell family since the late 1830s, which malts all its own barley on its floors and does every stage on site through to bottling. The 10 Year Old, medium peated, distilled two and a half times and bottled at 46% ABV, is the Campbeltown benchmark.
picks.note: Campbeltown has three working distilleries (Springbank, Glen Scotia, Glengyle), so three of this group's five are labels: Longrow and Hazelburn are separately named malts of Springbank distillery and Kilkerran is the malt of Glengyle. The founders are given as the Reid family, Mitchell in laws, with the Mitchells from 1837; some sources say the Mitchells founded it. On site bottling rests on retail and reference sources. Library holds Springbank.

picks.why: The second working Campbeltown distillery, founded as Scotia by Stewart and Galbraith in 1832 and owned by the Loch Lomond Group since the 1990s. Double Cask, first fill bourbon cask malt finished in Pedro Ximenez sherry casks at 46% ABV, is the entry to its range.
picks.note: The Loch Lomond ownership year (1996) rests on one retail source. Victoriana, at cask strength (54.2% or 52.2% by source), and the 15 Year Old are its other core bottlings; the author may prefer the 15 as the flagship.

picks.why: The malt of Glengyle, the Campbeltown distillery the Mitchells of Springbank brought back into production in 2004 after decades shut; it is sold as Kilkerran because another company owns the Glengyle name. The 12 Year Old, first released in 2016, lightly peated, from bourbon and sherry casks at 46% ABV, is its flagship.
picks.note: A label of a distillery with another name: say so. The closure year (1925) and the 79 dormant years are given by different sources; keep to closed for decades. Glengyle runs a short season with the Springbank team; confirm before writing it.

picks.why: Springbank distillery's heavily peated malt, distilled twice and sold under its own name, so that one distillery makes three malts: Hazelburn unpeated, Springbank lightly peated and Longrow heavily peated. The no age statement Longrow is its standing bottling.
picks.note: A label of Springbank distillery: say so plainly. The strength of the standing bottling (46% is likely) and whether the label prints Longrow or Longrow Peated were not settled in this run; confirm on the producer's page. Some sources name a 10 Year Old as standard; confirm what is current. Library holds the distillery as Springbank.

picks.why: Springbank distillery's unpeated malt from air dried barley, distilled three times and sold under its own name. The 10 Year Old, ex bourbon cask malt at 46% ABV, shows how far one distillery's spirit moves with peat and the number of distillations.
picks.note: A label of Springbank distillery: say so plainly. Hazelburn bottlings are released irregularly; confirm the 10 Year Old is current. Library holds the distillery as Springbank.

alternates.why: A cask strength Glen Scotia in the style of a nineteenth century Campbeltown malt; a second bottling of a picked distillery, offered because Campbeltown has no sixth working distillery.
The aged core Glen Scotia at 46% ABV; a second bottling of a picked distillery, offered because Campbeltown has no sixth working distillery.

left.why: A category, not a kind of producer: every single malt in this lane belongs to it, and its groups are the six regions (Speyside, Highland, the Islands, Lowland, Islay, Campbeltown), so a separate group of five would only repeat their picks.

The Lowland benchmarks list names Cameronbridge, which is a grain distillery and not a malt house, and Rosebank, which closed in 1993 and only resumed distilling in 2023 with no core bottling yet; neither is picked, and the author may wish to correct the list. Kingsbarns and Lindores Abbey are picked in their place.
Campbeltown has three working distilleries and every label they make is either picked or offered; both alternates are therefore other bottlings of Glen Scotia, not sixth and seventh houses.
